tracks.title: The rename test
tracks.text: Lesson one point four — specs. This one is a sub-lesson, under workbook… and the question it opens with is small enough to feel like a trick. Take a workbook — a brand book called nike dot html — and rename it. Call it final-v2, paren three. Call it untitled, with no extension at all. Now… what broke? [curious] Nothing. The desktop app still recognises it. The installer still trusts it. The social card still builds. That refusal to break — that is the whole lesson. Because every other file on your machine knows itself by its name or its first few bytes. A Word file is dot docx. A PDF starts with the letters percent P D F. A program opens with a magic number. Rename them wrong, and tools get confused. A workbook can't play that game — its entire premise is, just an HTML file. So identity had to go somewhere a rename can't reach… inside the file.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A spec is the inline, machine-readable self-description a workbook carries… in a typed script tag, with the id workbook-spec. Its name, its kind, its shape — written where the browser won't run it. The marker, not the filename, is the format. And the runtime says this in its own words. The module that defines the format opens with three lines of comment. First — a workbook is one HTML file with an inline script, id workbook-spec, the self-description. Second — and the Org source it tangles from. Third — format is identified by the inline marker… not the filename. That's the law, written at the top of the file that enforces it.

tracks.title: Anatomy of the marker
tracks.text: Anatomy of the marker. The marker is three things wearing one tag. First… the id — workbook-spec. The known name every reader looks for. This is the handle, not the filename. Second… the type — application slash json, or text slash org. A type the browser can't execute, so it ships the bytes and never runs them. Zero runtime cost. Third… the payload — the self-description itself. Name, kind, columns, slug. An open map, different for every kind of workbook. And here's why it's a script tag, and not a meta tag, and not a comment. A meta tag holds one short string. A comment is invisible to the page. But a script with a type the browser won't run… is the one place in HTML you can stash a whole document — JSON, or Org — as pure data the page carries but never executes. [excited] Free cargo. So the test every reader runs is just one branch. Picture it: a file comes in, any name, any extension. Does it carry the script with id workbook-spec? If yes — it's a workbook. Readable, catalogable, installable. If no — it's just a web page. It still opens, it still runs… it's only unrecognised.

tracks.title: Twenty-four lines, two languages
tracks.text: Twenty-four lines, two languages. The format test is small enough to read aloud. Here's the whole parser. A function called spec, that takes some HTML. It runs one regular expression — find a script tag with id workbook-spec, capture everything inside. If it matches… decode that inside as JSON. If it doesn't match… return, error, no spec. That is it. One regex to find the marker. One decode to read it. On success you get the map — toolkit, rev. With no marker, error no spec. The whole module is twenty-four lines, and the test is two regexes — the second one finds an embedded source block we'll meet shortly. [curious] And here's the proof the contract is real, and not just an Elixir quirk. The desktop app ports it into Rust… byte for byte. Same regex. A function called read-spec, returning an optional value — something, when it parses, nothing, when the marker is missing or the JSON is broken. Two languages. One contract. Picture the two sitting side by side. Elixir calls it spec, Rust calls it read-spec. Elixir exposes a module function, Rust exposes a command named workbook-spec-read. Elixir returns ok-map or error-no-spec, Rust returns something or nothing. The verdict of that pairing — the format survived a full language port… because it was never more than, find the marker, read the payload. One honest footnote. Those Elixir functions have no callers inside the runtime yet — the live reader today is the desktop port and the test suite. Defined and proven… just not wired into the runtime itself. We'd rather tell you that, than imply more reach than there is.

tracks.title: How a folder becomes a library
tracks.text: How a folder becomes a library. This is a depth rung — skip it and the next part still lands. But it's where the marker stops being a definition and becomes a behaviour. The desktop app has to turn a folder of files into a library you can browse. And it asks exactly one question — is this a workbook? Picture the walk as a short pipeline, left to right. It starts with the package folders on disk. Step one — walk them for files ending in dot html or dot htm. That's a cheap extension pre-filter. Step two — scan each of those files in parallel for the marker, using read-spec. Step three — the ones that pass become library entries… a path, and a title. And the title comes from the spec's own title field, falling back to the filename when the spec doesn't name one. So in the running app, is a workbook is not a guess, and not a list — it is literally, carries a parseable workbook-spec. Now — that extension filter is the one place a filename matters at all. And it isn't identity. It's economy. Opening a thousand image files looking for an HTML marker would be a waste, so the scan narrows the haystack by extension before it opens anything. The extension narrows the haystack. The marker is still the needle.

tracks.title: One marker, two dialects
tracks.text: One marker… two dialects. Same id. Two payload languages. Both real, both shipping. And the split is worth saying out loud — JSON is the machine contract. Text-org is the publishable record. Let me line the two up. The JSON spec uses the type application slash json, and its payload is a JSON object — producers are the brand books, the kanban mock, the toolkits, and it's read by the runtime and desktop readers. It decodes cleanly. The Org spec uses the type text slash org, and its payload is an Org headline with a properties drawer — every live learn page carries one, including this one, and it's read by the learn site's own JavaScript and the social-card builder. And the verdict that matters most — run the JSON reader against that Org payload, and it does not decode. It returns an error. [curious] One marker id… two dialects… and the JSON parser only speaks one of them. That's not a bug to hide — it's the shape of the thing. The id says, here is this file's self-description. What dialect lives inside… depends on who is meant to read it.

tracks.title: This page runs on its own spec
tracks.text: This page runs on its own spec. Here's the demo you can check from the address bar. The page you're hearing about did not get its headline, its kicker, its read-time, its table of contents, or its social card from hand-written HTML. It got every one of them… from its own spec block. Edit the record, the page follows. Let me read you the parent lesson's actual record — the same kind of block this page carries. It's a script, type text-org, id workbook-spec. Inside, a headline — star, page, what is a workbook. Then a properties drawer. Slug, workbook. Kind, learn. N-N, oh-one. Title one, try emailing. Title two, someone. Title three, your app. Chip, the unit. Hero, the hero image. End of drawer. And then a second headline — star star, o-g — with one bullet underneath… one dot html, interface, code and data. Now watch what reads it. The site's JavaScript grabs that block, pulls the properties with a small regex, and rebuilds the chrome. The N-N and the kicker become the hero kicker. Title one, two, and three become the three-line headline. The chip, the read-time — word count over two-ten — and the whole table of contents all come from that record and the real sections. Separately, the social-card builder reads the spec, and never the HTML around it — those o-g bullets become the lines printed on the card you saw when this page was shared. Picture that as a fan-out from one block — the spec feeds the browser script, which paints the kicker, the headline, the chip, the read-time, the table of contents. And the same spec feeds the card builder, which turns the o-g bullets into the card. [excited] And the site finds its own pages the same way — it greps the folder for files that contain the marker. There is no page list. Only the marker. So… View Source on this page, scroll to the very bottom, find the block. Everything framing this lesson came out of it.

tracks.title: The file carries its own making
tracks.text: The file carries its own making. Another depth rung. The spec says what the file is. A sibling marker can carry how it was made. The runtime declares the seam plainly — a script with id workbook-org holds the literate Org source that the HTML tangles from. Same regex shape… a plain Org payload. And the shipping version of that idea lives in the brand-book pipeline, where it's more than a seam — it's a hard contract. A brand book carries its whole source tree as a second inert script. Picture two tags, stacked. The first — the spec, type application-json, holding slug nike, title Nike brand book, and a created-at. The second — id, w-b-source-bundle, type application slash x-workbook-source, with attributes — data-format, json plus gzip plus base64. Data-version, one. Data-file-count, fourteen. And then a long run of base64. The whole Org source tree… serialised, compressed, encoded. Both tags ignored by the browser. The spec to identify the file. The bundle so the file carries its own making. And that data-version, one — that is not decoration. The unbundle command hard-rejects any tag that lacks it. [sighs] And there's a war story in why. An earlier pipeline forgot the version attribute… so every shipped book failed to unbundle. An audit caught it. And the fix wasn't a patch at each spot that emitted the tag — it was collapsing all three render paths onto one function that emits it, so the contract can never drift again. One emitter. One shape. No drift. The minimal version of the whole idea is the kanban mock — and you could paste it into any HTML file right now. A script, id workbook-spec, type application-json. Inside — name, Kanban Board. Version, oh point one point oh. Kind, app. And columns — Backlog, In Progress, Done. That's all it takes for a file to become a recognisable workbook.

tracks.title: Specs under signature
tracks.text: Specs under signature. A depth rung, and the place the spec stops being a convenience… and becomes trust. When a toolkit ships, it ships as a workbook — there is no separate toolkit package format. The runtime says it flatly — a toolkit is a workbook. Its spec is just one key… toolkit, rev… riding inside the HTML. And the install path can demand a signature. Now — because the spec lives inside the file's bytes, signing the file signs the spec. Picture the round trip. The author signs the HTML — and the spec rides inside the signed bytes. The book ships. The installer verifies the signature over the whole file. If it's intact… the toolkit registers. But if a single byte was tampered with — the spec, or anything else — the install refuses, with a bad-signature error. The marker that identifies the file… is the same bytes the signature protects. The signature itself is a separate inline marker — a provenance manifest in its own script block — and how it's built and checked is the signatures lesson's job, not this one. The point here is narrow, and worth holding. The spec is not the signature. But the spec is inside what gets signed.

tracks.title: Where the spec stops
tracks.text: Where the spec stops. The honest part. The spec is a strong idea with real edges, and the page would be dishonest without them. There are four. First — there is no schema. A spec is an open map. The keys are per-kind convention, not a validated contract. A kanban board carries name and columns. A toolkit carries one key. A brand book carries slug and capture metadata. A learn page carries Org properties. Nothing enforces which keys appear — flexibility, bought at the price of a guarantee. Second — the runtime reader has no callers inside the runtime yet. The desktop port is the live consumer today. Defined and proven… not yet wired. Third — it's a regex, not an HTML parser. A literal closing-script tag inside a payload would cut it off early. JSON escaping makes that a non-issue in practice — but it's the real constraint, and pretending the parser is sturdier than two regexes would be a lie. And fourth — the marker gates recognition, not rendering. The published site serves a workbook whether or not it carries a spec. The marker decides whether something is recognised — scanned, catalogued, installed — never whether it renders. [curious] And the proof is one click away. The downloadable hello-workbook dot html carries no spec block at all. It opens. It runs. Perfectly. It just wouldn't show up in the desktop grid scan… because nothing told the scan it was a workbook. The file works. It's only unrecognised. And that one wrinkle is the cleanest statement of what the spec is even for.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] What goes in a spec? Whatever the kind needs — it's an open map, not a fixed schema. Kanban carries name and columns. A brand book carries slug and metadata. A toolkit carries one key. A learn page carries Org properties. Readers take what they understand and ignore the rest. Do I need one for the file to open? No. A workbook with no spec opens and runs fine — hello-workbook ships without one. You need the spec to be recognised, not to render. Why a script tag, and not a meta tag or a comment? Because the payload is a whole structured document, and a typed, non-running script is the one place HTML lets you carry that as data — addressable by id. Is the spec what gets signed? Not by itself — the signature is its own block. But the spec lives inside the file's bytes, and the signature covers the whole file… so signing the file signs the spec along with it. And — JSON or Org, which do I write? Both are real — pick by who reads it. JSON is the machine contract. Org is the publishable record. The id is the same… the dialect just follows the reader.

tracks.title: Back up to the workbook
tracks.text: So that's the spec. One inert script tag — that is somehow the format test, the catalog record, the install identity, and on this site, the record a page renders itself from. The browser never runs it. The filename never decides anything. Rename the file to whatever you like… and the file still knows what it is. [curious] The way back up is short. This sub-lesson sits under one parent — workbook, lesson one — the anatomy this spec describes. From there, the spec leads outward — to bundles, the container around the file. To signatures, the block that signs the bytes the spec rides in. And to org, the grammar a page's spec is written in. But start with the parent. Everything here is just the workbook… learning to say its own name.
